title: WHY DID GOD’S LAW MENTION SEX WITH A GRANDDAUGHTER? THE DISTURBING TRUTH BEHIND LEVITICUS 18:10
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD’S LAW MENTION SEX WITH A GRANDDAUGHTER? THE DISTURBING TRUTH BEHIND LEVITICUS 18:10

One of the Bible’s most uncomfortable commandments reveals something terrifying about human sin, something heartbreaking about the vulnerable, and something breathtaking about the God who refuses to abandon the wounded.
There are Bible verses that comfort you.
Verses you underline. Verses you frame on your wall. Verses you whisper when life becomes unbearable.
And then there are verses that make you stop reading.
Not because you don't believe in God.
But because you cannot believe what you just read.
Leviticus 18:10 is one of them.
It speaks about a grandfather and his granddaughter. About sexual boundaries within a family. About something so disturbing that most people would rather turn the page than ask why God addressed it.
And perhaps the most unsettling question is not why the Bible mentions such a thing.
Perhaps it is why human beings needed to be told.
Think about that.
Why would a holy God need to tell His people that a granddaughter was not someone to be sexually exploited?
What kind of world made that commandment necessary?
And what does this ancient passage have to say to a generation where some of the deepest wounds are still inflicted by people who were supposed to provide safety?
Stay with me.
Because this is not merely an article about an uncomfortable Old Testament law.
It is about the difference between love and exploitation.
Between authority and abuse.
Between the shame that belongs to the sinner and the shame that victims have been forced to carry.
And ultimately, it is about Jesus Christ, who entered a world filled with broken families, hidden wickedness, and wounded people—not to excuse evil, but to confront sin and bring redemption.
Before we reach the end, you may discover that the most disturbing part of this passage is also the reason it deserves to be read.
Listen carefully to what Scripture actually says.
“The nakedness of thy son's daughter, or of thy daughter's daughter, even their nakedness thou shalt not uncover: for theirs is thine own nakedness.” — Leviticus 18:10, KJV
There it is.
No attempt to disguise the subject.
No pretending such evil could never happen.
God's law explicitly prohibited sexual relations involving one's granddaughter, whether she was the daughter of one's son or one's daughter.
But to understand this verse faithfully, we must understand its language, its setting, and the larger biblical story.
The Hebrew text reads:
עֶרְוַת בַּת־בִּנְךָ אוֹ בַת־בִּתְּךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה עֶרְוָתָן כִּי עֶרְוָתְךָ הֵנָּה
Transliteration:
ʿErwat bat-binkha ʾo bat-bittekha lo tegalleh ʿerwatan ki ʿerwatkha hennah.
A close translation is:
“The nakedness of your son's daughter or your daughter's daughter you shall not uncover—their nakedness—because their nakedness is your own.”
The expression עֶרְוָה (ʿervah) means nakedness, and the phrase לֹא תְגַלֵּה (lo tegalleh) means “you shall not uncover.”
But this is not merely a rule about accidentally seeing someone without clothing.
In the context of Leviticus 18, “uncovering nakedness” is a Hebrew expression used in prohibitions concerning sexual relations.
The chapter establishes boundaries around sexual conduct, particularly within family relationships.
And the command concerning a granddaughter is unmistakable.
A family relationship must never become an excuse for sexual access.
A position of authority does not grant ownership over another person's body.
Blood relationship does not make exploitation acceptable.
The command does not merely concern social embarrassment.
It marks a moral boundary.
And it is a boundary that must not be crossed.
But why was this law given to Israel?
We need to go back to the beginning of the chapter.
God speaks to Moses and instructs Israel:
“After the doings of the land of Egypt, wherein ye dwelt, shall ye not do: and after the doings of the land of Canaan, whither I bring you, shall ye not do.” — Leviticus 18:3, KJV
Israel had come out of Egypt and was being prepared to live in a land inhabited by other peoples.
God was calling His covenant people to a distinct way of life.
Not every practice of the surrounding nations was to become Israel's practice.
Not every cultural custom was morally acceptable.
Not every human desire deserved to be obeyed.
The chapter addresses prohibited sexual relationships, adultery, child sacrifice, and other conduct Israel was commanded to reject.
But we must be careful.
Leviticus 18:10 does not give us a documented historical case of a particular grandfather abusing his granddaughter.
Nor does the verse prove that this exact offense was widespread in every surrounding nation.
The text gives a prohibition, not a statistical report.
We do not need to invent a horrifying historical story to make Scripture powerful.
The command itself is serious enough.
God was establishing boundaries that would govern His people's conduct, including relationships within their own households.
And that matters because the family was supposed to be a place of responsibility, provision, and protection.
Imagine a young girl growing up in a household where adults are expected to care for her.
She should be able to approach her family without fear.
She should be able to trust the people entrusted with her well-being.
Her vulnerability should call forth greater responsibility from the adults around her, not become an opportunity for exploitation.
Now imagine that trust being violated.
Imagine the confusion.
The fear.
The silence.
The possibility that the very person responsible for protecting her is the one causing her harm.
This is not a claim that Leviticus 18:10 describes a particular victim's experience.
It is an illustration of why such boundaries matter.
Because sexual wrongdoing within a family is never simply about the private desires of the person committing it.
It can devastate the life of someone who trusted that person.
And here is something we must never misunderstand.
The shame of sexual abuse belongs to the abuser, not to the person who was abused.
A child does not become morally guilty because an adult violated a boundary.
A victim does not become spiritually contaminated because someone committed evil against them.
The commandment identifies forbidden conduct. It does not authorize blaming those who suffer from it.
That distinction is essential.
Because throughout history, some wounded people have been made to carry shame that was never theirs.
Some were told to remain silent to protect the family name.
Some were pressured to forgive without truth, safety, or accountability.
Some were even made to feel that speaking about abuse would dishonor God.
But hiding evil is not holiness.
Protecting an offender's reputation at the expense of the vulnerable is not righteousness.
And forgiveness must never be twisted into permission for continued harm.
Scripture says:
“Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction.” — Proverbs 31:8, KJV
And again:
“Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy.” — Psalm 82:3, KJV
The God of Scripture does not call His people to protect wrongdoing through silence.
He calls them to justice.
He calls them to truth.
He calls them to care for the vulnerable.
If this subject touches something painful in your own history, please hear this with all the tenderness it deserves.
You are not responsible for another person's decision to violate you.
You do not have to describe your trauma publicly to prove that it happened.
You do not have to confront an abuser alone.
And if a child is currently being harmed, protecting that child and involving appropriate safeguarding or legal authorities must take priority over preserving anyone's reputation.
God's Word should never become a weapon used to keep the wounded trapped.
Now consider another question.
Why does the verse say, “For theirs is thine own nakedness”?
The final Hebrew phrase is:
כִּי עֶרְוָתְךָ הֵנָּה
Ki ʿerwatkha hennah.
Literally, “For they are your nakedness.”
This language is connected to the close family relationships addressed throughout the chapter.
Leviticus 18 repeatedly uses the language of nakedness to identify sexual boundaries within kinship.
The granddaughter is not a stranger outside the family structure.
She belongs to the man's own line of descent.
That close relationship is precisely why sexual relations are forbidden.
We should not force the Hebrew to say more than it says.
The expression is not a technical modern psychological description of abuse, nor is it a claim that the granddaughter is the grandfather's property.
It is a kinship-based explanation for the prohibition.
The family connection itself places the relationship outside legitimate sexual boundaries.
And there is something deeply revealing about that.
Human beings have a frightening ability to rationalize what they desire.
We can rename selfishness as love.
We can disguise control as concern.
We can call manipulation protection.
We can use affection, familiarity, or authority to blur boundaries that should remain unmistakably clear.
That is why God's commands matter.
They confront us with the truth that our desires are not the final measure of righteousness.
God's holiness is.
But there is another danger here.
We can read Leviticus 18:10, recoil at the severity of the sin, and congratulate ourselves for never committing it.
Then close the Bible feeling morally superior.
Yet the purpose of Scripture is not to let us stand above everyone else's sin.
It is to bring us before the holiness of God.
The person who has committed a terrible wrong must face the seriousness of that wrong.
The person who has never committed that wrong must still recognize their own need for grace.
And the person who has suffered because of another's wickedness must not be placed in the same category as the offender.
These are not interchangeable spiritual conditions.
Sin must be named truthfully.
Victims must be treated justly.
And all of us must understand that God's grace is not a denial of His righteousness.
This brings us to the New Testament.
Because someone might ask, “If Christians are under grace, does Leviticus 18 still matter?”
The answer requires more than simply quoting a verse.
Christians understand the Mosaic law in light of the person and work of Jesus Christ and the teaching of His apostles.
The New Testament does not place Gentile believers under the entire covenantal legal system given to ancient Israel.
Yet it unmistakably continues to condemn sexual immorality and violations of proper sexual boundaries.
Paul writes:
And in 1 Thessalonians 4:3, he says:
“For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication.”
The Greek word translated “fornication” in these passages is πορνεία (porneia), a broad term referring to sexual immorality.
The New Testament's moral vision does not treat sexual conduct as irrelevant simply because salvation comes through grace.
Grace does not transform evil into good.
Grace calls people away from sin and toward Christ.
And this is where the story becomes intensely personal.
Because the Gospel does not begin with humanity proving that it is worthy.
It begins with the truth that humanity needs a Savior.
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
But we must understand that verse properly.
It teaches the universal reality of human sin.
It does not mean every person has committed the same offenses.
It does not mean a victim is guilty of the abuse committed against them.
And it certainly does not erase the distinction between someone who harms and someone who is harmed.
Instead, it reminds us that no human being can earn salvation through personal moral perfection.
We need Jesus.
And what a Savior He is.
When Jesus walked among people, He did not reserve His compassion for those society considered respectable.
He drew near to the broken.
He welcomed the repentant.
He exposed hypocrisy.
He confronted those who burdened others while refusing to bear those burdens themselves.
And He spoke with extraordinary seriousness about causing vulnerable people to stumble.
In Matthew 18:6, Jesus warned of severe judgment for those who cause “one of these little ones which believe in me” to stumble.
That warning must not be reduced to a vague sentimental slogan.
Jesus was speaking about the gravity of leading vulnerable believers into sin and spiritual ruin.
But His words reveal something unmistakable.
He does not regard the destruction of the vulnerable as a small matter.
The Lord Jesus is not indifferent to the misuse of power.
And His compassion is not weakness.
It is holy.
It is truthful.
It is courageous.
Think about the woman in Luke 7 who approached Jesus in tears.
Her sins were known publicly.
People judged her.
They looked at her past and assumed they understood her worth.
But Jesus spoke about forgiveness and faith.
He said:
“Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace.” — Luke 7:50, KJV
That woman was not presented as a victim of the offense described in Leviticus 18:10, and we should not pretend her story is identical.
But her encounter reveals the heart of the Gospel.
Jesus receives repentant sinners through faith.
He offers forgiveness that human respectability cannot purchase.
And He gives peace where shame once ruled.
Now consider the cross.
The Roman soldiers mocked Him.
His enemies accused Him.
His disciples scattered.
And the Son of God suffered publicly.
Jesus was not being punished for His own wrongdoing.
He was sinless.
He willingly gave Himself for sinners.
As 1 Peter 3:18 declares:
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God.”
There is the center of Christianity.
Not merely a moral code.
Not merely a collection of ancient prohibitions.
Not merely the command to become a better person.
Jesus Christ, the righteous One, giving Himself to reconcile sinners to God.
And when He rose from the dead, He demonstrated that sin and death would not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
This is why our message is not simply that terrible things happen in the world.
Our message is that Jesus Christ has entered this fallen world to redeem.
But redemption must never be confused with pretending that wrongdoing did not happen.
If you have committed sexual wrongdoing, genuine repentance does not consist of saying a few religious words while continuing the same behavior.
It requires turning away from sin.
It requires honesty.
It requires accepting appropriate consequences.
Where another person has been harmed, repentance does not entitle the offender to renewed access, private reconciliation, or the victim's trust.
Accountability and protection remain necessary.
The Gospel offers forgiveness through Christ, but forgiveness is not a loophole through which someone can escape responsibility.
And if you are someone who has been wounded, the Gospel does not demand that you call your suffering good.
It does not require you to return to an unsafe environment.
It does not command you to trust someone who has demonstrated that they are dangerous.
Jesus can bring healing without requiring you to deny reality.
And healing may involve prayer, trustworthy pastoral support, professional trauma-informed care, and time.
Sometimes a great deal of time.
You are not spiritually defective because the healing process is difficult.
You are not less faithful because you still struggle.
You are not required to produce a beautiful testimony before you are ready.
The Lord who knows the truth of what happened is not confused by your tears.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.”
That promise does not mean every wound disappears immediately.
It means the brokenhearted are not beyond God's concern.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this desperately needs to know.
God's presence is not reserved for people whose lives look undamaged.
His mercy is not available only to those who can explain their pain neatly.
His grace reaches into places people are afraid to speak about.
There may be someone reading this who has carried a secret for twenty years.
Someone who learned to smile while feeling unsafe inside.
Someone who hears the word “family” and feels grief instead of comfort.
Someone who has spent years asking why the people who should have protected them did not.
And perhaps there is someone else reading who knows they have committed a serious wrong and has spent years hiding behind religion.
The message to these two people cannot be identical.
To the wounded, we say: what was done to you does not make you guilty.
To the unrepentant offender, we say: stop hiding, stop harming, tell the truth, and submit to appropriate accountability.
To both, we point to Jesus Christ—not as a way to erase the distinction between guilt and innocence, but as the One in whom truth, justice, mercy, and hope meet.
And this is why Leviticus 18:10 still deserves our attention.
Because it forces us to confront a truth our world desperately needs.
Not every relationship called love is loving.
Not every person who claims authority is trustworthy.
Not every family secret deserves protection.
And not every silence is peace.
Sometimes silence is the place where injustice survives.
Sometimes truth is the beginning of protection.
Sometimes the most faithful thing a person can do is refuse to cooperate with a lie.
And sometimes the beginning of healing is hearing someone say, without hesitation, “What happened to you was wrong.”
There is a reason the Bible does not consist only of pleasant stories.
Scripture records murder.
Betrayal.
Adultery.
Oppression.
Incest.
Sexual violence.
The failures of kings.
The corruption of leaders.
The rebellion of ordinary people.
Not because God delights in wickedness.
But because the Bible tells the truth about a fallen world.
It refuses to build a beautiful religious illusion over the reality of human sin.
And it refuses to leave humanity without the promise of redemption.
From Genesis to Revelation, the story moves toward Jesus Christ.
The promised offspring who would defeat the serpent.
The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.
The risen Lord who calls sinners to repentance and faith.
The coming King who will judge with righteousness.
And the Savior who declares:
“Behold, I make all things new.” — Revelation 21:5, KJV
Notice what He says.
Not merely, “I make things appear new.”
Not, “I teach people to pretend the past never happened.”
Not, “I call evil good.”
He makes all things new.
That is the Christian hope.
A new creation.
A final defeat of evil.
A world in which death, sorrow, crying, and pain will no longer rule.
Revelation 21:4 points toward that glorious future.
And until that day, Christians are called to live as people who belong to the coming Kingdom.
People who tell the truth.
People who protect the vulnerable.
People who repent when they sin.
People who refuse to excuse exploitation.
People who love their neighbors not merely with words, but through righteous action.
Because holiness is not simply about what we refuse to do.
It is also about whom we choose to protect.
And if we claim to love Jesus while ignoring the suffering of those entrusted to our care, we have misunderstood something fundamental about following Him.
The command in Leviticus 18:10 may be ancient.
But the moral responsibility it confronts is painfully contemporary.
And here is the question I want you to carry with you.
When people encounter us as followers of Jesus, do they find a safe place for truth?
Or do they discover that our concern for appearances is stronger than our concern for righteousness?
That question should trouble every church.
Every parent.
Every spiritual leader.
Every believer.
Because the credibility of our witness is not measured only by how loudly we proclaim God's Word.
It is also revealed in whether we are willing to obey Him when obedience becomes costly.
And now I want to speak directly to the person who almost stopped reading.
Maybe the title made you uncomfortable.
Maybe you wondered why a Christian page would discuss something so disturbing.
Maybe you thought faith was supposed to focus only on encouraging things.
But sometimes the most loving thing we can do is open a difficult passage and refuse to look away.
Because there are people who have never heard someone explain these verses without shame, sensationalism, or cruelty.
There are believers who are afraid to ask honest questions about Scripture.
There are young Christians whose faith is being challenged by people who quote disturbing Bible passages without context.
There are wounded people who wonder whether God sees what happened behind closed doors.
And there are families who need to learn that biblical faithfulness includes protecting those who cannot protect themselves.
That is why careful, Christ-centered teaching matters.
Not because every article will be comfortable.
But because the truth of God's Word is worth understanding.
If this article has helped you see Leviticus 18:10 more clearly, don't allow the conversation to end here.
You do not need to tag anyone whose private experience this subject might expose.
And if you want to join the conversation, I would genuinely love to hear your answer to this question:
What should the Church do to make sure that people who have been wounded find truth, safety, and the compassion of Christ rather than silence and shame?
If your own heart is weary, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.”
You do not owe anyone your personal story.
And if you have experienced God's healing in some area of your life and want to encourage others, you may comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Sometimes a few honest words can remind another believer that they are not alone.
Not because it is pleasant to revisit difficult subjects, but because careful biblical understanding matters, and some passages deserve more than a quick reaction.
Return to the Scriptures.
Read the surrounding chapter.
Test what has been written here against God's Word.
Ask thoughtful questions.
Keep learning.
We want people to encounter Scripture with reverence, honesty, compassion, and an unwavering focus on Jesus Christ.
That is also why I want to extend a personal invitation.
Our desire is to make biblical learning, encouragement, and spiritual nourishment accessible to people who genuinely want to grow deeper in Jesus Christ.
It is voluntary financial support for the ongoing work of producing biblical teaching, maintaining discipleship resources, and reaching more people with the message of Jesus Christ.
Scripture teaches the importance of cheerful, willing generosity:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
And that is the spirit in which this invitation is made.
Not guilt.
Not fear.
Your giving should be prayerful, voluntary, and responsible, without neglecting your family, local church, or other important obligations.
You glorify God through faith in Christ, obedience, love, truth, generosity, and the whole life you offer to Him.
But supporting faithful Gospel work can certainly be one meaningful way to participate.
The greatest purpose remains the same.
Helping people know Jesus.
Helping believers grow in Scripture.
Helping the weary find biblical encouragement.
Helping those with questions discover thoughtful answers.
And helping more people hear that forgiveness, repentance, and new life are found in Christ.
We are not trying to put a price on the Gospel.
We are seeking to steward resources so the message can continue reaching people.
Because somewhere there is a believer wrestling with a Bible passage they do not understand.
Somewhere there is a young person asking whether Christianity can withstand difficult questions.
Somewhere there is a wounded soul wondering whether God cares about the injustice they endured.
And somewhere there is a sinner who needs to hear both the seriousness of repentance and the astonishing mercy offered through Jesus Christ.
They deserve more than shallow answers.
They deserve the truth.
And the truth leads us back to the cross.
So let us return one final time to that uncomfortable verse.
Leviticus 18:10.
A command that many people would prefer never to discuss.
A prohibition involving one of the closest relationships in a family.
A reminder that human beings need moral boundaries, even where love and trust should already exist.
The verse does not explain every historical circumstance behind its inclusion.
It does not answer every question about human suffering.
And it does not by itself tell the whole story of redemption.
But within the whole counsel of Scripture, it helps us see something important.
God's holiness is not indifferent to what people do with their bodies, their relationships, or their power.
The vulnerable are not outside His concern.
Evil does not become righteous simply because it happens within a family.
And the Gospel does not ask us to choose between truth and grace.
In Jesus Christ, we encounter the One who is “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).
Truth that refuses to call evil good.
Grace that welcomes the repentant sinner.
Mercy that reaches toward the brokenhearted.
Justice that does not disappear because someone speaks religious words.
And hope that reaches beyond the worst things this fallen world can do.
Maybe you came here expecting an explanation of one strange Bible verse.
But perhaps you are leaving with a deeper question.
What kind of people should we become if we truly belong to Jesus?
People who refuse to hide behind appearances.
People who protect rather than exploit.
People who repent rather than rationalize.
People who tell the truth without abandoning compassion.
People who refuse to confuse forgiveness with permission to harm.
People who remember that the cross is both a declaration of the seriousness of sin and the immeasurable love of God.
And people who know that no amount of darkness can overthrow the final victory of the risen Christ.
That is the hope we carry.
That is the truth worth sharing.
That is the Gospel worth supporting.
And that is why we will keep pointing people back to Jesus.
Because the final word over those who belong to Him will not be spoken by their shame, their wounds, their failures, or the sins committed against them.
The final word belongs to the Savior who died, rose again, and will make all things new.
What evil tried to bury in silence, Christ can bring into the light—and the wounds this world cannot undo will not have the final word in His Kingdom.
